title: Teaching AI and higher education
author: Bryan Alexander
source: aiandacademia.substack.com (AI, academia, and the Future), October 17, 2026
summary: Futurist Bryan Alexander gives a mid-semester report on the graduate seminar on AI and higher education that he teaches in Georgetown's Learning, Design, and Technology program. The course is structured as a "challenge class," where students and instructor set major questions together, such as how colleges should prepare students for a post-AI workforce, how AI changes research, and how to redesign assessment. He describes the mix of methods used to investigate each challenge, including curated readings in Canvas, shared writing in Google Docs, whiteboarding in Miro and small-team proposals to university leaders. A recurring "AI current events" exercise and hands-on use of AI tools for brainstorming and writing run through the sessions. Themes from the class include AI augmenting rather than replacing academic work, the need for higher education to act more energetically, and anxiety over job prospects. He closes with plans for more hands-on agentic computing, a unit on AI's broader social context, and a student-designed final assessment.
points: The seminar is built as a challenge class in which students and instructor co-define the major questions and the structure emerges over the semester.
Each challenge is investigated through readings, asynchronous discussion, shared writing, whiteboarding and team proposals aimed at university leaders.
A recurring AI current events exercise keeps the course connected to fast-moving news such as safety incidents and policy developments.
Students reported using AI for brainstorming, idea development and improving their writing, and the class leaned toward AI that augments rather than replaces academic work.
Next steps include hands-on work with agents, a unit on AI in society and politics, and letting students decide the final assessment.
quotes: AI has been, by far, the leading topic of interest among all of these audiences, from campus board members to professors, university librarians to students.
It’s also a challenge class, meaning we (students and I) structure the semester by determining a series of major ideas and questions, which we then figure out how to investigate and build upon.
The class’ structure and operations emerge over time, collaboratively.
Students responded asynchronously in the Canvas discussion board to the prompts I posted there. Back in class, we did shared writing in Google Docs and did group whiteboarding in Miro.
AI to augment or enhance academic work, not replace it or people, was a leading theme.
There was also a sense that higher ed needs to act more energetically and creatively on AI, alongside concern about AI’s potential downsides.
This was such a valuable experience that I built in an “AI current events” exercise into each subsequent class meeting.
We don’t have a mid-term or final project or other assessment built in. I’d like to see what the students determine would be most appropriate for them at this point.
